876.title: The Vietnamese martyrs
876.hook: 117 martyrs from the 1700s and 1800s, most of them laypeople
876.howItsDone: The Church keeps the memorial of Saint Andrew Dung-Lac and companions, and Vietnamese Catholic communities, in Vietnam and abroad, honor the martyrs with Masses, processions and shrines.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Korean church, begun by readers with no priest in the country. Your line was laypeople first. What page did you read on your own? A new week starts, and we stay in Asia, a little further south. Day eight hundred seventy-six.

Soldiers stand around a wooden cross laid flat in the dirt of a courtyard. A prisoner is led in, a farmer, or a catechist, or a mother with children waiting at home, and told: walk across it, step on it, and you can go. Tradition says this test was used again and again in Vietnam's persecutions. It asks for one step. It doesn't ask for a speech or a signature. Just a foot on two pieces of wood. Today, the people who wouldn't take that step.
screen: `A CROSS IN THE DIRT.` → `STEP ON IT AND GO HOME.` → `ONE STEP.`

segments.voice: First, who they were. The Catholic faith in Vietnam was carried by missionaries, and by Vietnamese catechists who taught in the villages. When rulers turned against it, Christians were hunted, churches were destroyed, and families hid their priests. The martyrs the Church honors together include Vietnamese priests like Andrew Dung-Lac, Spanish and French bishops and missionaries, catechists, a soldier, a doctor, fishermen and farmers, and Agnes Le Thi Thanh, a mother who sheltered priests. Second, the step. For them, the choice came down to that cross in the dirt. Refusing it meant prison, beatings, and often death. Third, a letter. Paul Le Bao Tinh, a Vietnamese priest, wrote from his prison cell to young seminarians. He described chains, hunger and cruelty, and said the prison was like a picture of hell. And then he said he was not alone: Christ was with him, and he was full of joy. He asked them to pray for him, so he could stay faithful. Fourth, witnesses. Saint Paul asks, in Romans, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation? or distress? or famine? or nakedness? or danger? or persecution? or the sword?" And in Acts, Jesus tells his followers: "you shall be witnesses unto me." The Church calls its martyrs witnesses, the word Acts uses here. Pope John Paul II declared these Vietnamese martyrs saints together. Vietnam's Catholics still keep their feast, and their names.
screen: `FARMERS, PRIESTS, A MOTHER, A SOLDIER.` · `THE CROSS IN THE DIRT.` · `A LETTER FROM PRISON.` · `A MARTYR IS A WITNESS.` · then, large: `WHO THEN SHALL SEPARATE US FROM THE LOVE OF CHRIST?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold Vietnam in mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture a village church in Vietnam on a Sunday morning: motorbikes outside, children on the steps, the bell ringing. Then widen it: cities, rice fields, the coast, families scattered around the world. If you know a Vietnamese person, bring their face to mind. If you pray, you can pray for Vietnam and its Catholics, and for all who suffer for their faith today. If you don't, simply wish the people of Vietnam well. The bell holds the time.
The Vietnamese martyrs. Priests, catechists, mothers, soldiers and farmers who died rather than step on the cross, honored by the Church as saints together.
Your line: the vietnamese martyrs. Today, notice one small step you're asked to take against what you believe, and decide, quietly, which way your foot goes. Day eight hundred seventy-six.

877.title: The hidden Christians of Japan
877.hook: after the Nagasaki martyrs, families kept the faith in secret, with no priests, for generations
877.howItsDone: Catholics in Japan keep the feast of Paul Miki and his companions, and pilgrims visit the churches and villages around Nagasaki linked to the hidden Christians.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vietnamese martyrs: priests, catechists and families who held on under persecution. Did one of their names stay with you? Today, another coast, and a faith that went underground. Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

A small white figure of a woman holding a child sits on a farmhouse shelf in Japan. To a visiting official it looks like Kannon, a Buddhist figure of mercy. To the family who owns it, it is also Maria. Christianity has been banned. Missionaries have been sent away, and on a hill at Nagasaki, Paul Miki and his companions were crucified for the faith. After that, in fishing villages and on small islands, families went on praying anyway. Quietly. With no priests at all. Children grew up, had children, and passed it on. Today: the hidden Christians of Japan.
screen: `A MOTHER AND CHILD ON A SHELF.` → `THE FAITH IS BANNED.` → `NO PRIESTS AT ALL.`

segments.voice: Japanese has a name for them: kakure kirishitan, hidden Christians. Some historians keep that name for the groups who stayed apart after the ban was lifted, and call the families of the hidden years senpuku, underground. First, the hiding. The faith lived inside ordinary households: a figure on a shelf that could pass for something else, prayers said quietly at home, feasts kept without anyone outside noticing. Second, the laypeople. With no priests, there was no Mass and no confession. But the Church teaches that in need, anyone with the right intention can baptize. So villages chose baptizers, and the water and the words kept going. They kept a calendar of feasts, and prayers handed down by heart, called orasho. Third, the memory. With no books out in the open, prayers were learned by ear. Over the generations some words wore smooth, like stones in a river, a mix of Latin, Portuguese and Japanese sounds. Fourth, the return. When missionaries came back and built a church in Nagasaki, tradition says a group of villagers came to the French priest there, Bernard Petitjean, and a woman whispered that their hearts were the same as his. Then they asked him where the statue of Santa Maria was. Not every hidden community joined the Church again after that; some kept the ways they had guarded so long. In the Gospel of Luke, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus tells his disciples: "Fear not, little flock." A little flock, kept for generations by nothing but memory.
screen: `A FAITH BEHIND A SHELF.` · `LAY BAPTIZERS, PRAYERS BY HEART.` · `WORDS WORN SMOOTH BY MEMORY.` · `OUR HEARTS ARE THE SAME AS YOURS.` · then, large: `FEAR NOT, LITTLE FLOCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose a small faithful habit. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small thing you could do every day that holds what matters to you. A line said on waking. A sign of the cross. A minute of quiet before the phone. A thank-you before eating. Something so small nobody else would notice. If you pray, you can say a prayer you know by heart, slowly, the way those families kept theirs. If you don't, hold the habit in mind and see where it fits tomorrow. The bell holds the time.
The hidden Christians of Japan. Families who kept baptism, feasts and prayers alive in secret, without priests, generation after generation.
screen: `THE HIDDEN CHRISTIANS OF JAPAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: 250 years in secret. Today, do your small faithful habit once, where no one sees it, and keep it the way a family keeps something worth handing on. Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

878.title: Elizabeth Ann Seton (1774–1821)
878.hook: a widowed mother, a convert, a founder of schools, honored as a saint
878.howItsDone: Catholics in the United States keep Elizabeth Ann Seton's feast in early January, and Catholic schools often mark it with a Mass and stories of her life; pilgrims visit her shrine at Emmitsburg, Maryland.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hidden Christians of Japan, keeping baptism and prayer alive with no priests. Your line was 250 years in secret. Did your small habit happen? Today, a young widow in New York. Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

Her husband coughs through the night in a cold stone quarantine building on the coast of Italy, and she is the one nursing him. He is dying of tuberculosis. Their little daughter is with her; the other children are home in New York. She is American, she belongs to the Episcopal Church, and she reads her Bible. When her husband dies, an Italian Catholic family, the Filicchis, take her in. She goes to Mass with them and watches how they pray. Then she sails home a widow, with young children, little money, and a head full of questions. Her name is Elizabeth Ann Seton.
screen: `A QUARANTINE ROOM IN ITALY.` → `A HUSBAND DIES.` → `A CATHOLIC FAMILY TAKES HER IN.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. Back in New York, what drew her most was the Eucharist, the Catholic belief that Christ is truly present in the bread at Mass. She wrote about wanting to be near it. She was received into the Catholic Church, and friends and relatives pulled away. Help dried up. Second, the classroom. A widow with children had to earn a living, so she taught. A school she tried in New York struggled. Then she was invited to Baltimore, and there she opened a small school for girls. Later, in a valley at Emmitsburg, Maryland, she started another, where poorer children could learn alongside those who paid. Third, the sisters. Women came to join her, and she founded a religious community, the Sisters of Charity of Saint Joseph's. They began calling her Mother Seton. She did not stop being a mother at home, either; she was raising her own children through all of it, and she grieved the deaths of daughters she loved. Fourth, the saint. The Church canonized her, and Catholic schools across the United States name her as a patron. A teacher, honored as a saint. In the Gospel of Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "Suffer the little children, and forbid them not to come to me." She spent her last years doing that in a schoolroom, one lesson and one child at a time.
screen: `DRAWN BY THE EUCHARIST.` · `A WIDOW WHO TEACHES.` · `THE SISTERS OF CHARITY.` · `A TEACHER CANONIZED.` · then, large: `SUFFER THE LITTLE CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a teacher. Settle, and breathe. Let one teacher come to mind. A schoolteacher, a coach, a grandmother at a kitchen table, a boss who showed you how. Remember one thing they taught you that you still use. Hold their face for a moment. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, simply stay with the gratitude. When the bell rings, you might send them a message, or say their name to someone. The bell holds the time.
Elizabeth Ann Seton. A widow and a convert who opened schools for girls, founded the Sisters of Charity, and became Mother Seton.
Your line: mother seton. Today, thank one person who taught you something, out loud or in writing, and tell them what it was. Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

879.title: John Carroll (1789)
879.hook: the priests of a new country choose their own bishop, a friend of religious liberty
879.howItsDone: Catholics in the United States remember John Carroll at Baltimore's basilica and at Georgetown, and parishes in the United States pray for the nation at Mass on Independence Day and Thanksgiving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elizabeth Ann Seton, the widow who taught in a valley in Maryland. Your line was mother seton. Did you thank a teacher? Today, a priest from the same state, and a question about who chooses a bishop. Day eight hundred seventy-nine.

A letter goes from a small group of priests in the new United States to Rome, and its question is unusual. The country has just won its independence. Catholics there are a small group, often distrusted, scattered across farms and port towns. They have no bishop of their own. Rome could simply appoint one and send him over. Instead, the priests ask: may we choose? And the answer comes back yes. They gather, they vote, and they pick a Maryland man who had once been a Jesuit, a cousin of a signer of the Declaration of Independence. His name is John Carroll.
screen: `A NEW COUNTRY, NO BISHOP.` → `MAY WE CHOOSE?` → `THEY VOTE FOR ONE OF THEIR OWN.`

segments.voice: First, the loss. He trained as a Jesuit in Europe and was teaching there when the pope suppressed the Society of Jesus. His order, the life he had chosen, was dissolved. He came home to Maryland as a parish priest with no community, riding out to say Mass in family houses. Second, the revolution. When the colonies broke with Britain, he sided with independence. Congress even sent him along with Benjamin Franklin on a mission to Canada, hoping a Catholic priest might help win over Catholic Canadians. It didn't work, but it put him at the center of the new nation's life. Third, the bishop. Chosen by his fellow priests and confirmed by the pope, he became bishop of Baltimore, a diocese that stretched across the whole country. He gave much of his energy to schools: he founded the academy that became Georgetown. Fourth, the freedom. Carroll argued that the new republic should protect the conscience of every citizen, and that Catholics should be free to worship and to serve their country like anyone else. He saw the young nation's promise of religious liberty as something Catholics could hold to, not just tolerate. Saint Paul writes in the second letter to the Corinthians, in the Douay-Rheims: "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." Carroll's hope was a land where faith did not need a king's permission.
screen: `A JESUIT WITHOUT AN ORDER.` · `A PRIEST IN THE REVOLUTION.` · `BISHOP OF BALTIMORE.` · `FREEDOM OF CONSCIENCE.` · then, large: `WHERE THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD IS, THERE IS LIBERTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give thanks for one freedom, whatever country you call home. Settle, and breathe. Think of one freedom you used today without noticing. Speaking your mind. Walking into a church, a mosque, a temple, or none at all. Reading what you chose. Then think of someone, nearby or far away, who doesn't have that freedom. If you pray, you can pray for your country and for them. If you don't, simply hold both in mind, side by side. The bell holds the time.
John Carroll. The Maryland priest whose fellow priests chose him as their bishop, a founder of schools and a friend of religious liberty.
Your line: a new land. Today, use one freedom on purpose, and give thanks for it, or speak up once for someone who doesn't have it. Day eight hundred seventy-nine.

880.title: The Kingdom of Kongo
880.hook: Afonso I of Kongo, a devout Catholic king who wrote to Portugal to protest the slave traders
880.tomorrow: The slave trade and the Church
880.howItsDone: Catholics in Angola and the Democratic Republic of the Congo remember the old Kingdom of Kongo, and the ruins of the old cathedral at Mbanza Kongo are visited as a sign of that early Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Carroll, the bishop whose fellow priests chose him. Your line was a new land. Which freedom did you use on purpose? Today, a much older Catholic story, in central Africa. Day eight hundred eighty.

What does a king do when the Christian kingdom that sent him priests is also carrying off his people? This one writes. His letters, in Portuguese, go by ship from central Africa to the king of Portugal. He calls the Portuguese king his brother. He asks for priests, for teachers, for medicine, for books. And then the tone changes. Traders from Portugal, he writes, are seizing his people, free people, even his own nobles and relatives, and shipping them away. He asks his brother king to stop it. The man writing is a baptized Catholic, a ruler who built churches in his capital and prayed in them. His name is Afonso, king of Kongo.
screen: `LETTERS TO PORTUGAL.` → `PRIESTS, TEACHERS, BOOKS.` → `THEY ARE TAKING OUR PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: The Kingdom of Kongo sat along the great river that still carries its name. First, a faith chosen. When Portuguese ships arrived, Kongo's king and court were baptized. Afonso, born Mvemba a Nzinga, became a Christian, and studied the faith with the priests. Kongo was not conquered into the Church; its own rulers brought the faith in. Second, a Catholic court. As king, Afonso built churches in his capital, which came to be called São Salvador, Holy Savior. He set up schools and sent young Kongolese, among them his own son Henrique, to study in Portugal. Henrique was ordained, and later made a bishop. Third, the letters. Afonso's letters survive, and they are not polite paperwork. He tells the king of Portugal that merchants are carrying off his subjects, that the trade is emptying his land, and he asks that only priests and teachers be sent, not traders. Fourth, the cost. Kongo itself held captives and sold some, and in time Afonso settled for officials who checked whether each person sold had been lawfully enslaved. The trade did not stop. Kongo's faith did not stop either. For generations, Kongolese Catholics kept churches, feasts and lay leaders of their own, often with very few priests. At the end of the Gospel of Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus sends the apostles out: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations." In Kongo, the nation was teaching too: an African king reminding a European one that he had asked for teachers, not traders.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Catholics in Africa, or simply wish them well. Settle, and breathe. Remember Afonso, a believer asking his own Church to do right. Then bring to mind one person you know, or know of, with roots in Africa: a neighbor, a coworker, a priest, a singer. Think of what they carry: a language, a song, a way of praying. If you pray, you can pray for the Church in Africa, and for the descendants of Kongo. If you don't, let your good wishes go out to them. The bell holds the time.
The Kingdom of Kongo. A central African kingdom whose rulers chose baptism, and whose Catholic king Afonso wrote to protest the slave traders.
Your line: an african kingdom. Today, look up Kongo on a map, find where São Salvador stood, and say Afonso's name once to someone. Day eight hundred eighty.

881.title: The slave trade and the Church
881.word: The slave trade and the Church
881.hook: popes condemned it, and yet Catholics took part; Gregory XVI condemned the trade outright in 1839
881.howItsDone: Catholics remember Peter Claver on his feast day, and some American dioceses and religious orders, including Jesuits, have studied and publicly acknowledged their own past in slavery, working with descendants on reconciliation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kingdom of Kongo, and King Afonso's letters asking Portugal for teachers, not traders. Your line was an african kingdom. Today we follow those ships, and look honestly at what the Church said and did. Day eight hundred eighty-one.

A ship docks at Cartagena, on the Caribbean coast of South America. In its hold are African men, women and children, chained, sick and terrified. On the dock a Spanish Jesuit is waiting with water, fruit, bandages and interpreters. He goes down into the hold. His name is Peter Claver, and he called himself, in Latin, the servant of the Africans forever. He cared for the people the ships brought for the rest of his life. And the ships kept coming, into a Catholic city, bought and sold by baptized men. Today's question starts on that dock.
screen: `A SHIP AT CARTAGENA.` → `A PRIEST GOES DOWN INTO THE HOLD.` → `THE SHIPS KEEP COMING.`

segments.voice: This is a hard story, told here in four parts. First, the permission. Earlier popes had issued letters granting the kings of Portugal the right to conquer non-Christian lands and to reduce their peoples to servitude. Some historians read those letters as part of the story of how the Atlantic trade grew. Second, the protests. Other popes and Catholics spoke against the enslaving of Indigenous peoples and Africans: priests like Claver, a few theologians, and popes in letters of their own. Third, the practice. Catholic merchants, colonists, and even religious orders and dioceses held enslaved people, bought them and sold them. In the United States, Jesuits in Maryland sold the people they held to pay their debts, and their descendants are still telling that story today. Fourth, the letter. Pope Gregory the Sixteenth, in a letter of eighteen thirty-nine, recalled the earlier condemnations and forbade any cleric or layperson to defend the trade in Africans as permissible, or to preach or teach it in any way. Even then, some Catholics read his words as condemning the trade but not slavery itself, and went on as before. Condemned and still done. Saint Paul writes to the Galatians, in the Douay-Rheims: "There is neither Jew nor Greek: there is neither bond nor free." The words were there all along. Some Catholics today name this history as a wound, and a warning that a church can say the right thing and still fail to live it.
screen: `PAPAL GRANTS TO PORTUGAL.` · `PRIESTS AND POPES WHO PROTESTED.` · `CATHOLICS WHO BOUGHT AND SOLD.` · `GREGORY XVI'S LETTER.` · then, large: `NEITHER BOND NOR FREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make room for a hard history. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people carried on those ships, people whose names most of us will never know. You don't have to picture the details. Just let them be people, with mothers and children and songs. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for their descendants today. If you don't, simply hold them in silence. When the bell rings, choose one thing to learn about the slave trade where you live. The bell holds the time.
The slave trade and the Church. Popes who granted permission, popes and priests who protested, Catholics who took part, and a pope's condemnation that did not end it.
screen: `THE SLAVE TRADE AND THE CHURCH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: condemned and still done. Today, read one page of a history you didn't know, about your own town, your church or your country. Day eight hundred eighty-one.

882.title: Palestrina
882.hook: the composer whose music showed Trent that many voices can serve the words
882.howItsDone: Catholic cathedral and parish choirs sing Renaissance polyphony, including Palestrina's Masses and motets, at solemn Masses, alongside Gregorian chant.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the slave trade and the Church: permissions, protests, and a pope's letter. Your line was condemned and still done. What history did you read? Today, at the end of a heavy week, something to listen to. Day eight hundred eighty-two.

A small choir stands in a stone chapel in Rome. One voice starts a line. A second comes in a moment later, singing the same tune a little higher. Then a third, a fourth, until the room is full of separate lines weaving over and under each other, and none of them is the melody, and all of them are. It sounds like one breath. Bishops at a church council had worried that music like this buried the words of the Mass. The composer at the center of the story people tell about it was a choirmaster from a hill town near Rome. The town was called Palestrina, and so was he.

segments.voice: Today's word is polyphony: many voices, each singing its own line at the same time. First, the worry. At the Council of Trent, bishops complained that some church music had become showy, mixed with worldly songs, with so many voices tangled together that nobody could hear the prayer. The council's decree barred music that was lascivious or impure from the Mass, and some bishops pressed for words that could be clearly understood. Second, the legend. A story grew up afterward: the council was ready to ban polyphony altogether, until Palestrina wrote a Mass so clear and so beautiful that it changed their minds. That Mass carries the name of a pope, Marcellus. Historians aren't sure the story happened that way. But the story stuck because the music fits it. Third, the music. In Palestrina's writing the voices take turns, so the words come through, then blend again. Nothing shouts. No single singer is the star. Fourth, the place it holds. The Second Vatican Council gave Gregorian chant pride of place in the Roman liturgy, and said that other kinds of sacred music, especially polyphony, are not excluded. Choirs from cathedrals to small parishes still sing Palestrina at Mass. Psalm one hundred fifty ends, in the Douay-Rheims: "Let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia." Every spirit, every voice, each on its own line, and one prayer underneath them all.
screen: `TRENT WORRIES ABOUT THE WORDS.` · `THE LEGEND OF THE MASS THAT SAVED IT.` · `VOICES TAKE TURNS SO WORDS COME THROUGH.` · `CHANT FIRST, POLYPHONY WELCOME.` · then, large: `LET EVERY SPIRIT PRAISE THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Palestrina. If you can, put on a recording of his music now, quietly, maybe the Mass named for Pope Marcellus. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to follow every line. Choose one voice, high or low, and stay with it for a while. Then let go and hear them all together. If you pray, let the music carry your prayer. If you don't, simply listen. No recording? Sit with the sounds around you, and pick out one at a time. The bell holds the time.
Polyphony. Many voices, each singing its own line at once, woven so the words of the prayer still come through.

Your line: many voices, one word. This week: martyrs in Vietnam, hidden families in Japan, Mother Seton, John Carroll, the king of Kongo, a hard history, and Palestrina. Today, listen for one voice you usually talk over. Day eight hundred eighty-two.
